title: Wine, the King, Women, or Truth?
sum: King Darius gives a vast feast for his whole empire, from India to Ethiopia, and goes to bed. While he sleeps, his three young bodyguards make a game: each will write down the one thing that is strongest, and the king and his three great nobles will judge which is wisest. The prize is a royal one: purple, gold, a gold-bridled chariot, a seat second only to the king and the title of Kinsman. The first writes "Wine," the second "The king," and the third "Women," adding, "but truth wins over all things."

When the king wakes, he calls his court to hear the young men explain themselves. The first speaks for wine. It makes king and orphan think alike, makes the poor feel rich, wipes out memory of grief, debt and duty, and turns friends to swords; and when the drinkers wake, they remember nothing. His praise is really a picture of wine's power to make people forget, and it sets up the speeches to come.
readings: The chapter follows the pattern of Joseph, Daniel and Esther: a royal feast, a sleepless king, a contest of wisdom, and a young Jew who will win. The reader already knows the answer will not be wine.

What is strongest? is an old riddle, and each speaker argues by examples. The third answer comes in two parts, women and truth, and Böhler reports that the truth speech is widely seen as an addition to an older riddle of three (see the note on 3:12).

views.O: Orthodox Bibles print 1 Esdras (the Russian Synodal Bible has it as the second book of Ezra), and Mihăilă counts it among the books beyond the Hebrew canon that the Orthodox reckon, one of two of them that Catholics do not accept; see the note on 4:13.
views.H: Swete called the story, in its present form, "certainly unhistorical," because Zerubbabel belonged to the age of Cyrus, and Torrey (1910) held that it was a separate tale set into the history by a later hand. Darius I's own inscription at Behistun lists twenty-three lands, not 127; this book shares the number with Esther 1:1. Hypatoi (3:14) is a Greek word of the writer's own age.
views.J: The contest is not in the Jewish Bible, but Josephus retells it at length and names Zerubbabel from the start, as an old friend of the king and one of his guards (Antiquities 11.32-35).
views.S: There is no parallel to chapters 3-4 in Chronicles, Ezra or Nehemiah. Ezra moves from the halt under Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:7-24) to the prophets under Darius (Ezra 5:1). 1 Esdras fills that space with the contest.
views.W: In the West the chapter was known through the Latin Vulgate's appendix, where the book is 3 Esdras, and through the Apocrypha of English Bibles (the KJV of 1611 includes it). The Church of England's Article VI names "The Third Book of Esdras" among the books the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not "to establish any doctrine."

deep.b: Ezra and Haggai say that Zerubbabel led the return and was governor, but never how he got the post (Ezra 2:2; Haggai 1:1). The contest answers that question with a story: a young Jew at Darius's court wins the king's favor by wisdom, and asks not for riches but for Jerusalem. Torrey (1910) counted the tale with the wisdom writing of its age; as the book has it, it becomes a lesson about what is truly strong.

echoes: Esther 1:1-9; Daniel 6:1; Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29-35; Genesis 41:42; Daniel 5:7; Daniel 5:29

settings.by: Three young bodyguards of King Darius
settings.to: Each other, at night, while the king sleeps after his feast
settings.when: After Darius's great feast for his empire
settings.why: To win the king's favor by a contest of wisdom; the terms (written sayings, sealed, judged by the king and three nobles, rich prizes) make the outcome a public royal decision that the king must honor.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were Greek-speaking Jews; the book names no place or date for itself (the book's opening pages give the proposals). For Jews under foreign rulers, the tale showed a Jew winning a king's favor by wisdom and using it for Jerusalem, and it ranked truth, and the God of truth, above wine, kings and women. The first reader we can name is Josephus, who retold the contest as history (Antiquities 11.31-67).

settings.to: King Darius and his whole court: nobles of Persia and Media, satraps, generals, local governors and chief officers
settings.when: When the king had woken, in the hall of audience before his court (3:13-14)
settings.why: To show that wine is strongest because it overpowers the mind of everyone, king and orphan alike. Spoken to men who had just feasted and drunk, it is half praise and half warning, and it prepares the hearers for the speeches that will rank wine below the king, women and truth.

title: Great Is Truth
sum: The second guard argues for the king: men rule land and sea, but the king rules men. They kill, build, plant and pay taxes at his word, while he eats and sleeps under guard. Then the third guard, Zerubbabel, argues that women rule even the king. Women bear kings and raise the vine growers; men leave father and country for a wife, rob and risk lions for the woman they love, and lose their minds for women. He has even seen the king's concubine Apame take his crown and slap him, while the king gapes and sweet-talks her.

Then he turns to truth. Earth, sky and sun are great, but truth is stronger than all things. Wine, the king, women and all people are unjust and will perish; truth stays, lives and rules forever, with no favorites and no bribes, and it ends in the blessing of "the God of truth." The people shout, "Great is truth, and it is strongest!" Darius offers the winner anything he wants. Zerubbabel asks the king to keep his vow to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple and to send back the vessels. Darius grants it in full: letters for safe travel, cedar from Lebanon, freedom from tax, money for the temple and its offerings, pay for priests, Levites and guards. Zerubbabel thanks the God of the fathers, and the exiles in Babylon feast for seven days.
readings: The four speeches climb a ladder: wine overpowers the mind, the king commands bodies, women win hearts, and truth outranks all, because it belongs to God. The chapter is a short lesson in what is truly strong, close to the Wisdom books.

Ezra puts the return under Cyrus and the work under Darius after a search of the archives (Ezra 6:1-12), and has no contest. Swete called the story, in its present form, "certainly unhistorical," because Zerubbabel belonged to the age of Cyrus, and it was Cyrus, not Darius, who decreed the rebuilding. Read as history, the chapter shows what a Jewish writer hoped a foreign king would grant.

Christian readers have heard in the praise of truth a pointer to the God who is truth, and later to Christ, "the way, the truth and the life" (John 14:6). Swete called the Latin form of the cry, magna est veritas et praevalet, "the immortal proverb" this story gave.

views.O: Orthodox Bibles print 1 Esdras (the Russian Synodal Bible has it as the second book of Ezra), and Mihăilă counts it among the books beyond the Hebrew canon that the Orthodox reckon, one of two of them that Catholics do not accept; see the note on 4:13.
views.H: Böhler notes that the truth speech (4:33-41) is widely seen as a later addition, and argues instead that the women and truth speeches together make one argument, with an idea of truth close to Qumran: 1 Esdras, written in the 100s BC, uses truth against the "liars" of the Hasmonean leadership. Torrey (1910) judged "this was Zerubbabel" (4:13) a later addition. The decree (4:47-57) is a Jewish writer's picture of an ideal royal grant; its "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia" (4:48) is the name of the Greek age.
views.J: Josephus retells the speeches in the same order, naming Apame's father "Rabsases Themasius" and putting the people's verdict as "it was truth alone that had immutable strength" (Antiquities 11.54, 57). He gives Darius's grant for the temple as fifty talents (11.60-61). The book is not in the Jewish Bible.
views.S: There is still no parallel in the Hebrew books. Darius's grant overlaps with his decree in Ezra 6:6-12 (money for the building and the daily offerings) and with Artaxerxes' letter in Ezra 7:12-26 (freedom from tax for temple staff). The cedar from Lebanon recalls Ezra 3:7. The note on 4:44 shows that the vessels, already sent home in 2:10-14, are sent again here.
views.W: Latin readers knew the cry of 4:41 in the Vulgate's form, magna veritas et praevalet. Catholic and Protestant churches do not count 1 Esdras as Scripture; Article VI of the Church of England lists "The Third Book of Esdras" among the books the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not "to establish any doctrine."

deep.h: What the truth speech says about God
deep.b: The speech never names God until its last words, "Blessed be the God of truth!" (4:40). Before that it gives truth the powers the Bible gives God: it lives and rules forever (4:38; Psalm 117:2), shows no favoritism and takes no bribe (4:39; Deuteronomy 10:17), judges without injustice (4:40; Deuteronomy 32:4), and has strength, royal power and majesty (4:40; 1 Chronicles 29:11). The closing blessing keeps truth from becoming a rival god: it is God's truth. This is why Jewish and Christian readers could take the speech as praise of God without changing a word.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the winner proves his own point
deep.b: This is Claude's reading. Zerubbabel wins by arguing that truth is strongest, and then he does what truth does: he asks the king for nothing for himself and holds him to his own vow (4:43-46). The king who could command anything (4:7-9) and was ruled by a concubine (4:29-31) is finally ruled by his own word. The tale enacts its thesis.

echoes: Genesis 2:24; Ecclesiastes 1:5; Psalm 19:4-6; Psalm 117:2; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 32:4; 1 Chronicles 29:11; Daniel 2:20-23; Ezra 6:6-12; Ezra 7:12-26; Obadiah 1:11-14; Psalm 137:7; John 14:6

settings.when: After the speech for wine, in the hall of audience
settings.why: To flatter the listening king by proving that he is strongest: armies, farmers and taxpayers obey his every word. Before the king himself the argument is safe, but the story lets its ending (a king who only eats and sleeps) undercut it.

settings.to: King Darius and his court, with the king's concubine Apame as the speech's example
settings.when: After the speech for the king
settings.why: To overturn the first two answers: women give birth to kings and to those who make wine, and men give up wealth, family and even sanity for them. Daring before the king, it uses the king's own court life as proof, which makes the nobles look at one another (4:33).

settings.to: King Darius, his nobles and all the people present
settings.when: At once after the speech for women
settings.why: To rank all three earlier answers below truth, which is lasting and just, and to end by blessing the God of truth. Before a Persian court it praises a value every hearer could honor; for Jewish readers it confesses Israel's God as the source of truth. The people's shout makes the verdict public.
views: The truth speech as an addition
Böhler reports that the truth speech is widely seen as a later addition to the tale (see the note on 3:12).
The truth speech as the goal
Böhler argues that the women and truth speeches only together make one argument, by a Jewish author of the 100s BC (abstract of his 2014 article).
settings.readers: Josephus, the first reader of the book we can name, retells this speech and the people's verdict, "it was truth alone that had immutable strength" (Antiquities 11.55-57).

settings.when: After the king offers him whatever he asks
settings.why: To turn the king's favor to Jerusalem by reminding him of his own vow to rebuild the city and temple and return the vessels. He asks nothing for himself.

settings.to: His treasurers, local governors, generals and satraps; the governors of Coele-Syria, Phoenicia and Lebanon; the Jews going up to Judea
settings.why: A royal grant: safe conduct, cedar, freedom and tax relief for the Jews, money for the temple and its daily offerings, support for priests, Levites and city guards, and the return of the vessels. It binds Persian officials to help, not hinder, the rebuilding.

settings.to: God, "the King of heaven," facing Jerusalem
settings.when: As he leaves the king's presence
settings.why: To give the victory and wisdom back to God, as Daniel did (Daniel 2:20-23), so that the court success is not his own.

title: The Return, the Altar and the Foundation
sum: Chosen by their tribes, the heads of families set out with their households, escorted by a thousand of Darius's horsemen and a band of drums and flutes. The book gives the leaders: the priest Jeshua, a Joakim who is called son of Zerubbabel, and "the one who spoke wise words" before Darius in his second year. Then it copies the great list of returnees from Ezra 2, in Greek forms of the names and with many numbers changed, ending with the same total, 42,360, and the gifts for the house of God.

In the seventh month the people gather by the east gate. Jeshua and Zerubbabel set up the altar, keep the Feast of Booths and the regular offerings, and hire workers and Phoenician timber men. In the second year the foundation is laid, with priests' trumpets, Levites' cymbals and the hymn of God's kindness and glory. The old men who had seen Solomon's temple weep so loudly that the trumpets cannot be heard. Then the neighbors, settled by an Assyrian king, ask to help build; Zerubbabel and Jeshua refuse, and the neighbors stop the work for as long as Cyrus lives, until the reign of Darius.
readings: From 5:7 the chapter follows Ezra 2:1-4:5 line by line, so the interest is in the differences: Greek names, changed numbers, an exact date for the founding (5:55), foreigners at the altar (5:49), and weeping that drowns the trumpets (5:62).

The chapter joins the contest story (5:1-6, under Darius) to the Ezra history (5:7-70, which ends "until the reign of Darius"). Read as one story, it seems to go back from Darius to Cyrus; read as a seam, it shows how the book was made (see the note on 5:70).

views.O: Orthodox Bibles print 1 Esdras (the Russian Synodal Bible has it as the second book of Ezra), and Mihăilă counts it among the books beyond the Hebrew canon that the Orthodox reckon, one of two of them that Catholics do not accept; see the note on 4:13.
views.H: The three copies of the list (Ezra 2, Nehemiah 7, 1 Esdras 5) can be set side by side to see where copyists lost or changed figures. Torrey (1910) read the "wise words" of 5:6 as the gloss that joins the contest to the list. The return under Darius in 5:6 conflicts with Ezra 1-3.
views.J: Josephus follows 1 Esdras here too: the old men's weeping drowns the trumpets (Antiquities 11.83), the neighbors are Cuthites settled by "Shalmanezer" (11.85), and the leaders refuse them partnership but not worship (11.86-87). He gives the 7,337 servants, 245 singers, 435 camels and 5,525 beasts of this chapter (11.72).
views.S: None of the 63 verses from 5:7 to 5:70 that have a parallel (5:55 has none) is word for word the same as the site's Ezra 2:1-4:5, because the Greek nearly always differs a little; the Plain keeps Ezra's wording wherever the Greek says the same thing. The closest differ by one word or number (5:27, "temple singers"; 5:35, 372 for 392). The differences are in names (Phoros for Parosh, Hattharias for the title "the governor"), numbers (Adonikam 37 for 666), additions (twelve years and up, 5:41; the Sabbaths, 5:51; a dated founding, 5:55; "two years," 5:70) and changed meaning (foreigners joining at the altar, 5:49; the weeping drowning the trumpets, 5:62; "we alone," 5:68).
views.W: The KJV Apocrypha printed this chapter in its own numbering (73 verses where Swete has 70). The votive Mass for the election of a pope, as printed in a set of parish propers, takes its offertory from 5:40, citing "3 Esdræ": no one may share the holy things until a high priest (pontifex) arises "in showing and truth" (in ostensionem et veritatem).

deep.h: The two dates of the return
deep.b: Ezra places the return and the altar under Cyrus and the finishing of the temple under Darius (Ezra 6:15). 1 Esdras places Zerubbabel's journey after the contest in Darius's second year (5:6) but then follows Ezra word for word, including the line that the work stopped "the whole time King Cyrus was alive" until Darius (5:70). Chapter 6 then begins again in Darius's second year with Haggai and Zechariah (6:1). There are two ways to read this: Torrey (1910) held that the contest was set into an older history and the seam left unsmoothed; or the compiler meant 5:7-70 as a look back at the first return under Cyrus, told after the story of how Zerubbabel came. Josephus places the contest in Darius's first year and the hindrance under Cyrus and Cambyses (Antiquities 11.33, 88).

echoes: Ezra 2:1-4:5; Nehemiah 7:6-73; Nehemiah 8:1; Nehemiah 12:10; 1 Chronicles 3:17-19; Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:3; Haggai 2:18; Zechariah 4:9; Exodus 28:30; Psalm 136:1; 2 Kings 17:24

settings.what: The list of those who returned
settings.by: The book's narrator, restating the register of Ezra 2
settings.why: A family register: it records which clans, towns, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants came back, and who could not prove their line. Lists like this decided who could serve as a priest and who belonged to the people (5:38-40).
settings.readers: Josephus, who followed this book, repeats its figures for servants, singers, camels and beasts of burden (Antiquities 11.72).

settings.what: The ruling on the priests without proof
settings.to: The men of the families of Hobbia, Hakbos and Jaddus, who claimed the priesthood but could not show their line
settings.when: At the return, after their family record could not be found (5:38-39)
settings.why: To keep the holy things for priests of proven line until a priest arose wearing the Showing and the Truth, the Urim and Thummim, who could settle the claim by God's answer. The ruling leaves the question open rather than closing it for good.

settings.by: Some of the heads of families
settings.to: God, at the temple site in Jerusalem
settings.when: When they reached the temple of God in Jerusalem
settings.why: To bind themselves to raise the house again on its site, as they were able, and to give gold, silver and priests' robes for the work. In Ezra the gifts are freewill offerings handed over (Ezra 2:68-69); here they are vows, promises to God that the givers must keep.

settings.by: The priests and the Levites of Asaph's family
settings.to: The LORD, before all the people
settings.when: When the temple's foundation was laid in the second year
settings.why: To give thanks with David's refrain (Psalm 136:1) that God's kindness and glory last forever; the old men's weeping shows that the joy was mixed with grief for the first temple.

settings.what: The neighbors' offer and the refusal
settings.by: The enemies of Judah and Benjamin, then Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the heads of families
settings.to: Each other: the neighbors to the returned leaders, the leaders in reply
settings.when: After the founding, when the neighbors hear the trumpets
settings.why: The neighbors claim the same Lord and long worship; the leaders answer that the commission to build was given to them alone by Cyrus. The exchange marks who belongs to the rebuilding community, a question that runs through Ezra and Nehemiah.
views: The leaders protected the worship of the LORD from a mixed cult (2 Kings 17:33).
The refusal turned willing neighbors into enemies, and the work stopped (5:69-70).
